sections.subtitle: Array in C
sections.description: In C, an array is a collection of similar data items stored in contiguous memory locations. It is a fundamental data structure used to store multiple values of the same type under a single variable name.

sections.subtitle: Declaration
sections.description:
Arrays are declared using the following syntax:

-->> dataType arrayName[arraySize];

dataType: Specifies the type of elements the array will store (e.g., int, float, char).
arrayName: The name given to the array variable.
arraySize: The number of elements the array can hold, specified within square brackets.

consoleBlock.c: -->> dataType arrayName[arraySize];

sections.subtitle: Array index
sections.description:
In programming, index refers to the position of an element within a data structure such as an array.

In both C and C++, zero-based indexing is used. This means that indexing starts from 0. So, for an array of size n, the valid indices range from 0 to n - 1.

int arr[5]; // An array of size 5

index --> 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

The indices for arr are:
arr[0]
arr[1]
arr[2]
arr[3]
arr[4]

This concept is important to understand to avoid common errors like accessing out-of-bound elements.

consoleBlock.c:
int arr[5]; // An array of size 5

index --> 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

The indices for arr are:
arr[0]
arr[1]
arr[2]
arr[3]
arr[4]

sections.subtitle: Multiple case discusion for Initialization & Assigning value into an array.
Multiple ways for Accessing Elements from an array
sections.description: Array elements are accessed using their index, which starts from 0 for the first element. The last element has an index of arraySize - 1

sections.subtitle: Types of Arrays
sections.description:
One-dimensional arrays: A single list of elements.

Multidimensional arrays: Arrays with more than one dimension, such as 2D arrays (matrices) and 3D arrays.C supports multidimensional arrays, which are arrays of arrays. They are useful for representing tables, matrices, and other structures with multiple dimensions.

consoleBlock.c:
int matrix[3][4]; // A 2D array (3 rows, 4 columns)
float cube[2][3][5]; // A 3D array

sections.subtitle: Key Characteristics
sections.description:
Fixed Size: Once declared, the size of an array cannot be changed.
Contiguous Memory: Elements are stored in adjacent memory locations.
Index-based Access: Elements are accessed using numerical indices.
Arrays and Functions:
Arrays can be passed to functions by passing the array name as an argument. The function definition must include square brackets to indicate that it is receiving an array.

sections.subtitle: Hello world!
Assignment operator in C
sections.description:
In programming, an assignment operator is used to assign a value to a variable. 

The most common assignment operator is the equal sign (=). 
Other assignment operators, like +=, -=, *=, and /=, are shortcuts for combining an arithmetic operation with assignment. 

For example, x += 10 is shorthand for x = x + 10.

sections.subtitle: Basic (=) Assignment Operators in C
sections.description:
Basic Assignment Operator (=):

The = operator assigns the value on the right-hand side to the variable on the left-hand side.

For example, int x = 10; assigns the value 10 to the variable x.
The left-hand side of the assignment must be an l-value, which is a location in memory that can be assigned a value (like a variable).
The right-hand side can be a value, another variable, or an expression that evaluates to a value.

sections.subtitle: All Compound (+=) Assignment Operators in C
sections.description:
Compound Assignment Operators:
These operators combine an arithmetic operation with assignment.


Examples include:
+=: Adds a value to a variable and assigns the result: x += 5 is the same as x = x + 5.
-=: Subtracts a value from a variable and assigns the result: x -= 3 is the same as x = x - 3.
*=: Multiplies a variable by a value and assigns the result: x *= 2 is the same as x = x * 2.
/=: Divides a variable by a value and assigns the result: x /= 4 is the same as x = x / 4.
%=: Calculates the modulo (remainder) of a variable divided by a value and assigns the result: x %= 3 is the same as x = x % 3.

These compound operators are often used for efficiency and readability, especially when updating a variable's value repeatedly.

sections.subtitle: Boolean  in C
sections.description: In C, the bool type represents boolean values, which can be either true or false. To use bool, you need to include the header file. Before the introduction of bool in C99, integers were used to represent boolean values, where 0 was false and any non-zero value was true.

sections.subtitle: Key points about Boolean  in C
sections.description:
Attach the header file first -->>  #include <stdbool.h>

true is equivalent to  --->> 1
false is equivalent to --->> 0
When printing a bool value using printf, it will be displayed as ---->>  1 or 0.

Boolean variables are commonly used in conditional statements and loops.

The size of a bool variable is typically -->>  1 byte.

sections.subtitle: Multiple use cases of bool with example
Comments in C
sections.description:
Comments in C are explanatory statements added to the code to enhance readability and understanding. The compiler ignores these comments during the compilation process.


C supports two types of comments:
1. Single-line
2. Multi-line.

sections.subtitle: Single-line comments
sections.description: These begin with // and continue until the end of the line.

consoleBlock.c:
// This is a single-line comment
    int x = 10; // This comment explains the variable declaration

sections.subtitle: Multi-line comments
sections.description: These begin with /* and end with */, and can span multiple lines.

Comments cannot be nested. They are treated as a single white-space character and can appear wherever white-space is allowed. They are useful for explaining code, making it more readable, and preventing the execution of code during testing.

sections.subtitle: Format Specifiers in C
sections.description:
Format specifiers in C are special tokens used with printf() and scanf() functions to specify:

--> The type of data being input/output
--> How the data should be formatted

They always begin with a % symbol followed by a format character.


Using the correct format specifier is crucial for accurate data input and output. Mismatched specifiers can lead to unexpected behavior or errors. For instance, using %d to print a float will result in incorrect output.

sections.subtitle: Basic Format Specifiers
Length Modifiers
Floating-Point Variations
Special Specifiers
Format Specifier Syntax
sections.description:
The full syntax is: %[flags][width][.precision][length]specifier


Common Flags:
- - Left-justify
+ - Force sign (+ or -)
- Space for positive numbers
0 - Pad with zeros
# - Alternate form (e.g., 0x for hex, decimal point for floats)


Width & Precision
%10s : Minimum width of 10 chars
%.2f : 2 decimal places
%10.3f : 10 width with 3 decimals

sections.subtitle: Key Differences Between printf() and scanf()
sections.description:
For floating-point numbers:

printf(): %f works for both float and double
scanf(): Must use %f for float, %lf for double


For strings:
scanf("%s") stops at whitespace
Use fgets() for strings with spaces


Safety:
Always specify maximum width for strings in scanf():

sections.subtitle: Implicit Type Casting in C
sections.description:
Implicit type casting in C, also known as automatic type conversion or type coercion, is a process where the compiler automatically converts a value from one data type to another without requiring explicit instructions from the programmer.


This conversion typically occurs when: 
 1. Assigning a value of a smaller data type to a variable of a larger data type
 2. Performing operations involving operands of different data types
 3. Passing arguments to functions


Implicit type casting aims to simplify coding and ensure type compatibility during operations, but it's crucial to understand the rules of type promotion to avoid unexpected behavior or potential data loss in certain scenarios (e.g., when converting a larger type to a smaller type, which would require explicit casting).

sections.subtitle: 1. Assigning Smaller to Larger Data Type ( Example 1)
Explanation of Example 1
sections.description:
char to int conversion

char letter = 'B';  // ASCII value 66
int ascii_value = letter;

A char is being assigned to an int variable
Characters in C are represented by their ASCII values (66 for 'B')
The compiler automatically promotes the 1-byte char to a 4-byte int

Output shows the ASCII value of 'B'

-------------------------------------------------------------

int to double conversion

int count = 100;
double precise_count = count;

An int is being assigned to a double variable
The integer value is automatically converted to floating-point representation
No loss of precision occurs in this case

Output shows the same value but now as a floating-point number

------------------------------------------------------------------------

float to double conversion

float temperature = 23.5f;
double precise_temp = temperature;

A float is being assigned to a double variable
This is a widening conversion (32-bit to 64-bit floating point)
The value remains the same but with potential for more precision

Output shows the same value but stored in a higher-precision format

sections.subtitle: Assigning Smaller to Larger Data Type ( Example 2)
Explanation of Example 2
sections.description:
short Limitations:

short is a 16-bit signed integer (range: -32,768 to 32,767).
200 * 300 = 60,000 exceeds short's max value (32,767).


What Happens?
C implicitly promotes short to int before multiplication.
a * b becomes int * int → No overflow because int (usually 32-bit) can hold 60,000.
Result stored in int result correctly.


Why No Overflow?
Integer Promotion Rule: Smaller types (char, short) are automatically promoted to int in expressions.

sections.subtitle: Assigning Smaller to Larger Data Type ( Example 3) -->> Complex ---> Do it youself --> Brainstorm
Explanation of Example 3
sections.description:
--->>> int Overflow in Intermediate Calculation (Before Assignment to long)  



Problem:
x * x = 50000 * 50000 = 2,500,000,000 (2.5 billion).
2.5 billion ➜ overflows int ➜ incorrect result before it's even assigned to y.
Even though y is a long int, the overflow already occurred in x * x. (Before assigned to long y, Overfows happend)
int (32-bit) max = 2,147,483,647 → Overflows before assignment to long.


Why?
C does not auto-promote int to long in arithmetic.
x * x is evaluated as int * int → Overflows first, then assigned to long y (too late!).


Expectation:
You might be thinking why the C compiler doesn't use implicit like example 2.

--> C promotes short to int automatically.
--> C does not promote int to long int during the multiplication.


Key Rule in C:-
In C, integer promotions happen only up to int or unsigned int during expression evaluation, not beyond that.


✅ Rule 1: Promote small types (e.g., char, short) to int
This is part of the "usual arithmetic conversions".
This is why short * short becomes int * int.

❌ Rule 2: No automatic promotion from int to long int
C does not automatically promote int to a larger type like long or long long during arithmetic.
So x * x is done entirely as int * int — and overflows if the result is too large

C tries to minimize surprises and keep type conversions predictable. Automatically promoting int to long or long long might change performance or precision unexpectedly in normal code, so it leaves that decision to you, the programmer.

sections.subtitle: Solution of Example 3 ( Force promotion with explicit casting )
( Example 4) -->> Complex ---> Do it youself --> Brainstorm
Explanation of Example 4
sections.description:
Mixed float and int Division (Truncation)

What Went Wrong?
numerator / denominator is int / int → truncates to 2 (integer division).
Only after truncation is the result converted to float (2.0).

sections.subtitle: Solution of Example 4 ( Force promotion with explicit casting )
sections.description:
Fix: Promote one operand to float:

Key Rule:
C does not auto-promote int to float in division unless one operand is floating-point.


You can follow this: 

Example	 Operation	        Issue	                         Implicit Rule	                  Fix
1	 short * short → int	No overflow (promotion)	         Small types → int	          Automatic
2	 int * int → long	Overflow (no promotion)	         No int → long auto-promotion	  Explicit cast
3	 int / int → float	Truncation (integer division)	 No int → float auto-promotion	  Cast one operand

sections.subtitle: Explanation of Example 1
sections.description:
int and float operation:

int items = 5;
float price = 12.99;
float total = items * price;


items is an integer (5) and price is a float (12.99)
Before multiplication, the compiler automatically converts items to float (5.0)
The multiplication is then performed as float × float
Result (64.95) is stored in the float variable total

Output: Total price: $64.95


char and int operation:

char initial = 'C';  // ASCII 67
int offset = 3;
char new_char = initial + offset;


initial is a char ('C' with ASCII value 67)
offset is an integer (3)
Before addition, initial is promoted to int (67)
The addition is performed as int + int (67 + 3 = 70)
Result is converted back to char (ASCII 70 = 'F')

Output: 'C' + 3 = 'F'



mixed float and double:

float radius = 5.5f;
double pi = 3.1415926535;
double area = pi * radius * radius;
radius is a float (5.5)


pi is a double (higher precision than float)
Before multiplication, radius is promoted to double (5.5 becomes 5.5 as double)
All calculations are done in double precision
Result is stored in the double variable area

Output shows higher precision: Area of circle: 95.0331777715




Key Points:

Type Promotion Hierarchy: In mixed-type expressions, values are converted to the "higher" type:
char → int → float → double


Arithmetic Conversions:
If either operand is double, the other is converted to double
Else if either operand is float, the other is converted to float
Else integer promotions are applied (chars/shorts become ints)

Assignment Conversions: When assigning to a variable, the result is converted to the variable's type

No Data Loss: These are widening conversions that preserve the original value



output:
Total price: $64.95
'C' + 3 = 'F'
Area of circle: 95.0331777715

sections.subtitle: Explanation of Example 1
sections.description:
Function:

print_cube(double num)

void print_cube(double num) {
    printf("Cube of %.2f is %.2f\n", num, num * num * num);
}

Takes a double parameter
Prints the number and its cube with 2 decimal places precision



print_bits(long value)

void print_bits(long value) {
    printf("Binary of %ld: ", value);
    for (int i = sizeof(long) * 8 - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        printf("%d", (value >> i) & 1);
    }
    printf("\n");
}
Takes a long parameter
Prints the binary representation of the number by examining each bit
Works by shifting and masking bits from most significant to least significant




Main Function:

int to double conversion

int side = 4;
print_cube(side);  // Implicit conversion from int to double

side is an int (4)
print_cube() expects a double
Compiler automatically converts int to double (4 → 4.0)

Output: Cube of 4.00 is 64.00



char to long conversion

char byte = 'A';  // ASCII 65
print_bits(byte);  // Implicit conversion from char to long

byte is a char ('A' with ASCII value 65)
print_bits() expects a long
Compiler promotes char to long (65 → 65L)

Output shows binary representation of 65 (depends on system, typically 64-bit)



float to double conversion

float amount = 12.5f;
print_cube(amount);  // Implicit conversion from float to double

amount is a float (12.5)
print_cube() expects a double
Compiler promotes float to double (12.5f → 12.5)

Output: Cube of 12.50 is 1953.12




Key Points:

Automatic Conversion: The compiler automatically converts arguments to match the function's parameter types when possible.

Type Promotion Rules:
--> Smaller types (char, short, int, float) are promoted to larger types (long, double)
--> No loss of precision occurs in these widening conversions

Binary Representation:
--> The print_bits() function shows how values are represented in memory
--> The conversion from char to long preserves the value but stores it in a larger space

Floating-Point Precision:
The conversion from float to double maintains the value but with higher precision

Output Differences:
--> Integer values show exact representations (4 → 4.00)
--> Floating-point values may show more precise results (12.5 cubed is actually 1953.125)



Output:
Cube of 4.00 is 64.00
Binary of 65: 0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000001000001
Cube of 12.50 is 1953.12
(Note: The exact binary output depends on your system's long size and endianness)

title: Increment and Decrement Operators in C (Pre and Post Variations)

sections.subtitle: Increment and Decrement Operators in C
sections.description: In C programming, increment (++) and decrement (--) operators are unary operators that increase or decrease the value of a variable by one, respectively. These operators are fundamental in various programming scenarios, such as loops, array traversals, and pointer arithmetic.

sections.subtitle: Increment Operator (++)
sections.description:
The increment operator increases the value of its operand by one. It can be used in two forms:

-->> Pre-increment (++x): Increments the value before it's used in an expression.
-->> Post-increment (x++): Increments the value after it's used in an expression.

sections.subtitle: Decrement Operator (--)
sections.description:
The decrement operator decreases the value of its operand by one. Similar to the increment operator, it has two forms:

-->> Pre-decrement (--x): Decrements the value before it's used in an expression.
-->> Post-decrement (x--): Decrements the value after it's used in an expression.

sections.subtitle: Pre-Increment (++x)
sections.description: In pre-increment, the variable is incremented first, and then the updated value is used in the expression.

sections.subtitle: Post-Increment (x++)
sections.description: In post-increment, the current value of the variable is used in the expression, and then the variable is incremented.

sections.subtitle: Pre-Decrement (--x)
sections.description: In pre-decrement, the variable is decremented first, and then the updated value is used in the expression.

sections.subtitle: Post-Decrement (x--)
sections.description: In post-decrement, the current value of the variable is used in the expression, and then the variable is decremented.

sections.subtitle: --->> Complex problem --->> Brainstorm --->> Give it a shot --->> Do it yourself

consoleBlock.c:
--->> Complex problem --->> Brainstorm --->> Give it a shot --->> Do it yourself


----->> What's the value of total? Find it out.


#include<stdio.h>

int main(){

int x=10,y=7,z=12;
int total = (x--)+(y++*3)+(++z)+(y++)+(--x*3)+(--z)+(z*3)-(--y*3);

printf("%d", total);

return 0;
}



/*
Output: 100
*/


----> Explanation

1. (x--)
Use x = 10, then decrement it → x = 9
Result: 10
2. (y++ * 3)
Use y = 7, then increment it → y = 8
Result: 7 * 3 = 21
3. (++z)
Increment z = 12 to 13, then use it
Result: 13
4. (y++)
Use y = 8, then increment it → y = 9
Result: 8
5. (--x * 3)
Decrement x = 9 to 8, then use it
Result: 8 * 3 = 24
6. (--z)
Decrement z = 13 to 12, then use it
Result: 12
7. (z * 3)
Use current z = 12
Result: 12 * 3 = 36
8. (--y * 3)
Decrement y = 9 to 8, then use it
Result: 8 * 3 = 24
--->> total = 10 + 21 + 13 + 8 + 24 + 12 + 36 - 24
= 100

sections.subtitle: Standard Input Function in C – scanf()
sections.description: In C, the standard input function reads data from the standard input stream, which is usually the keyboard. The most commonly used standard input function is scanf(). It reads formatted input from the user.

sections.subtitle: The scanf() function takes two types of arguments:
sections.description:
1. Format string
2. Addresses of variables

sections.subtitle: Format string:
sections.description:
Specifies the format of the input to be read. It includes format specifiers that begin with a percent sign (%). Some common format specifiers are:
%d: for integers
%f: for floating-point numbers
%c: for characters
%s: for strings

sections.subtitle: Addresses of variables:
sections.description: Specifies where the input data should be stored in memory. The address of a variable is obtained using the ampersand (&) operator.

In this example, scanf() is used to read a string, an integer, and a floating-point number from the user. The input values are stored in the variables name, age, and gpa, respectively. The printf() function then displays the stored values.
Other input functions in C include getchar(), which reads a single character, and fgets(), which reads a line of text. However, scanf() is the most versatile function for reading formatted input.

sections.subtitle: Loop in C
sections.description:
In C programming, loops are control flow statements that allow a block of code to be executed repeatedly.

C offers three main types of loops:
1. for
2. while
3. do while

sections.subtitle: For Loop
sections.description:
The for loop is typically used when the number of iterations is known in advance.

Its structure consists of three parts:
1. initialization
2. condition
3. update

Initialization: Executed only once at the beginning of the loop.
Condition: Evaluated before each iteration. The loop continues as long as the condition is true.
Update: Executed after each iteration, often used to increment or decrement a loop counter.

sections.subtitle: While Loop
sections.description:
The while loop executes a block of code as long as a given condition is true.

Initialization: Executed only once at the beginning of the loop.
Condition: Evaluated before each iteration. If true, the loop body is executed.
Update: Executed inside while block, often used to increment or decrement a loop counter.

sections.subtitle: Do While Loop
sections.description:
The do...while loop is similar to the while loop, but it executes the code block at least once before checking the condition.

Initialization: Executed only once at the beginning of the loop.
Condition: Evaluated after each iteration. The loop continues as long as the condition is true.
Update: Executed inside while block, often used to increment or decrement a loop counter.

sections.subtitle: While Loop & Do While Loop without Initialization & Update
sections.description: For this case, we often pass a variable or a Boolean value. Then we can check the condition.

sections.subtitle: Nested Loops
sections.description:
In C programming, a nested loop refers to a loop placed inside another loop. The inner loop executes completely for each iteration of the outer loop. This structure is commonly used when dealing with multi-dimensional data or when an action needs to be repeated multiple times in a structured manner.

Any type of loop (for, while, or do-while) can be nested within another loop of any type.

Nested loops are often used for tasks such as:
1. Iterating over 2D arrays: Accessing elements in rows and columns.
2. Printing patterns: Creating shapes or sequences of characters.
3. Solving matrix problems: Performing calculations on matrices.
4. Generating tables: Creating multiplication tables or other tabular data.

sections.subtitle: Loop Control Statements (Break & Continue)
sections.description:
1. break: Terminates the loop immediately.
2. continue: Skips the current iteration and moves to the next one.

In C programming, break and continue are control flow statements used within loops (for, while, do-while) to alter the normal execution flow.

Break Statement:
The break statement terminates the innermost loop it is enclosed within. When encountered, the program execution jumps to the statement immediately following the loop. It can also be used in switch statements to exit the case block.

In this example, the loop will terminate when i equals 5, and the output will be: 0 1 2 3 4 Loop terminated.


Continue Statement:
The continue statement skips the remaining code within the current iteration of the loop and proceeds to the next iteration. It does not terminate the loop but rather jumps to the loop's update expression (in for loops) or condition check (in while and do-while loops).

In this example, the loop will skip even numbers, and the output will be: 1 3 5 7 9 Loop completed.


Key Differences:
1. break terminates the loop entirely, while continue only skips the current iteration.
2. break can be used in switch statements, while continue is specific to loops.
3. break transfers control to the statement after the loop, while continue transfers control to the loop's update or condition check.

sections.subtitle: Extract last digit of a number
sections.description: Using the modulus operator, we can find out the last digit of a number.

consoleBlock.c:
int n;
scanf("%d", &n); // n = 7362 : wxyz

int z = n%10; // z = 2 (get the last digit)
n = n/10; // divide by 10 to remove the last digit. now n = 736

int y = n%10; // y = 6 (get the new last digit)
n = n/10; // divide by 10 to remove the last digit. now n = 73

int x = n%10; // x = 3 (get the new last digit)
n = n/10; // divide by 10 to remove the last digit. now n = 7

int w = n%10; // w = 7 (get the final digit)


/*

Extracted digits of 7362 as:

w = 7 (thousands place)
x = 3 (hundreds place)
y = 6 (tens place)
z = 2 (ones place)

*/

sections.subtitle: Standard Output Function in C – printf()
sections.description: In C, standard output refers to the stream of data that programs write to, typically displayed on the console. Several functions facilitate output operations, with printf being the most versatile and commonly used.

sections.subtitle: printf()
sections.description: This function prints formatted output to the standard output stream (stdout). It allows for the inclusion of variables, escape sequences, and format specifiers to control the appearance of the output.

sections.subtitle: putchar()
sections.description: This function outputs a single character to stdout.

sections.subtitle: puts()
sections.description: This function outputs a string to stdout, automatically appending a newline character at the end

sections.subtitle: fprintf()
sections.description: While primarily used for file output, fprintf can also write to stdout by specifying it as the output stream.

These functions provide different levels of control and convenience for outputting data in C programs. printf is suitable for complex formatting, putchar for single characters, puts for simple strings, and fprintf for directing output to specific streams, including stdout.

sections.subtitle: Statement in c language
sections.description: Statement: A statement in C programming is a command that instructs the computer to perform a specific action. It is the fundamental building block of a C program, and every program consists of a sequence of statements that are executed in a specific order.

sections.subtitle: There are different types of statements in C
Expression statements
sections.description: These are the most common type of statement and consist of an expression followed by a semicolon. They are used to evaluate an expression and optionally assign its value to a variable.

consoleBlock.c:
int x = 5;  // Declaration statement
    x = x + 10; // Assignment statement
    printf("%d", x); // Function call statement

sections.subtitle: Compound statements
sections.description: Also known as blocks, these statements group multiple statements together within curly braces {}. They are used to create a sequence of actions that are treated as a single unit.

sections.subtitle: Selection statements
sections.description: These statements allow the program to make decisions based on certain conditions. The most common selection statements are if, else if, and switch.

sections.subtitle: Iteration statements
sections.description: These statements allow the program to repeat a block of code multiple times. The most common iteration statements are for, while, and do-while.

sections.subtitle: Jump statements
sections.description: These statements allow the program to jump to a different part of the code. The most common jump statements are break, continue, and goto.

sections.subtitle: Labeled statements
sections.description: These statements are used to mark a specific location in the code with a label, which can then be used by goto statements.

sections.subtitle: Declaration statements
sections.description: These statements are used to declare variables, which are named storage locations that can hold data.

consoleBlock.c:
int age;         // Declare an integer variable named age
    float salary;    // Declare a floating-point variable named salary
    char name[50];   // Declare a character array (string) named name

sections.subtitle: Syntax in C
sections.description: Syntax : The syntax of C programming refers to the set of rules that govern how code statements are structured. These rules dictate the correct way to write code so that the compiler can understand and execute it. C syntax includes keywords, operators, punctuation, identifiers, and comments. It is case-sensitive, and most statements end with a semicolon. Whitespace is used to improve readability, but it is required for keywords and identifiers.

sections.subtitle: Key elements of C syntax
sections.description:
Header Files:
These are files containing declarations of functions and macros, typically included at the beginning of a C source file using the #include directive (e.g., #include <stdio.h>).


main() Function:
Every C program must contain a main() function, which serves as the entry point for program execution.


Statements and Semicolons:
Individual instructions or expressions in C are called statements, and most statements must be terminated with a semicolon (;).


Curly Braces {}:
These are used to define code blocks, such as the body of functions or control flow statements (e.g., if, for, while).


Variables and Data Types:
Variables are declared with a specific data type (e.g., int, float, char) to define the type of data they will store.


Comments:
Comments are used to add explanatory notes within the code and are ignored by the compiler. Single-line comments start with //, while multi-line comments are enclosed within /* */.


Keywords:
C has a set of reserved words (keywords) with predefined meanings that cannot be used as identifiers (e.g., if, else, while, for, return).


Identifiers:
These are names given to variables, functions, and other user-defined items. They must follow specific naming rules (e.g., starting with a letter or underscore, no special characters except underscore).


Tokens:
A C program is composed of various tokens, which are the smallest individual units of a program, including keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, and operators.

sections.subtitle: Variable in c
sections.description: In C, a variable is a named storage location in the computer's memory that can hold a value. It's like a container that can store data, which can be modified during program execution. Each variable has a specific data type that determines the kind of values it can hold, such as integers, floating-point numbers, or characters.

sections.subtitle: Keep in mind when using a variable
sections.description:
1. Declaration
2. Initialization
3. Data Types
4. Naming Rules
5. Scope

sections.subtitle: Declaration
sections.description: Before using a variable, it must be declared, specifying its data type and name.

consoleBlock.c:
int age;          // Declares an integer variable named 'age'
float salary;     // Declares a floating-point variable named 'salary'
char initial;     // Declares a character variable named 'initial'

sections.subtitle: Initialization
sections.description: Variables can be initialized at the time of declaration or later in the program.

sections.subtitle: Data Types
sections.description:
Data types in C can be broadly classified into the following categories: 


Basic (Primary) Data Types:
These are the fundamental data types built into the C language.

 int: Used to store whole numbers (integers).
 char: Used to store single characters.
 float: Used to store single-precision floating-point numbers (numbers with decimal points).
 double: Used to store double-precision floating-point numbers, offering higher precision than float.
 void: A special type indicating the absence of a value, often used with functions that don't return a value or as a generic pointer   
 type.


Derived Data Types:
These are constructed from the basic data types.

 Arrays: Collections of elements of the same data type, stored in contiguous memory locations.
 Pointers: Variables that store memory addresses of other variables.
 Functions: Blocks of code designed to perform a specific task, which can return a value of a certain data type or void.


User-Defined Data Types:
These are defined by the programmer using keywords provided by C.

 Structures (struct): Collections of variables of different data types grouped under a single name.
 Unions (union): Similar to structures, but all members share the same memory location, allowing only one member to hold a value at  
 a time.
 Enumerations (enum): Sets of named integer constants, improving code readability.


Data Type Qualifiers:
C also provides qualifiers that modify the basic data types:
 signed: Specifies that a variable can hold both positive and negative values (default for int, char).
 unsigned: Specifies that a variable can only hold non-negative values.
 short: Reduces the memory size of an int.
 long: Increases the memory size of an int or double.

sections.subtitle: Naming Rules
sections.description:
In C, variable names (also known as identifiers) must follow specific rules: they can only contain letters, digits, and underscores (_), must start with a letter or an underscore, are case-sensitive, cannot contain spaces or special characters, and cannot be a reserved keyword. 


Valid Variable Names:
 Letters, digits, and underscores: myVariable, count1, _value, name_of_student are all valid. 
 Start with a letter or underscore: _temp, data1, student_name are valid. 


Invalid Variable Names:
 Starting with a digit: 1variable is invalid.
 Containing spaces: my variable is invalid.
 Containing special characters: my.variable, student! are invalid.
 Being a keyword: int, float, return are invalid. 

Additional Considerations:
 Case sensitivity: myVariable and myvariable are treated as different variables. 
 No strict length limit: While there's no strict limit, excessively long names (over 31 characters) might cause issues in some compilers. 
 Descriptive names: It's good practice to use descriptive names that clearly indicate the variable's purpose. 
 Consistency: Following consistent naming conventions throughout a project improves readability and maintainability. 
 Keywords: Keywords are reserved words in C and cannot be used as variable names.

sections.subtitle: Scope
sections.description:
The scope of a variable defines where it can be accessed within the program.
Local variables: declared inside a block of code (e.g., a function) and are only accessible within that block.
Global variables: declared outside any function and are accessible throughout the program.
